questiontext.text: What happens in each round of Borůvka's minimum spanning tree algorithm?

answer.text: Every current component picks its cheapest outgoing edge, and all of those edges are added at once

feedback.text: Correct — Borůvka merges many components in parallel each round.

answer.text: A single global smallest edge is added, then the whole edge list is re-sorted

feedback.text: That resembles Kruskal's one-edge-at-a-time process, not Borůvka's per-component rounds.

answer.text: One tree grows by absorbing the cheapest crossing edge from a heap

feedback.text: That is Prim's single-tree growth, not Borůvka's.

answer.text: Vertices are explored depth-first and dead branches are pruned

feedback.text: That describes DFS, which does not build an MST by weight.

generalfeedback.text: Each Borůvka round has every component simultaneously choose its minimum-weight outgoing edge; all chosen edges are contracted together.

questiontext.text: Why does Borůvka's algorithm finish in O(log V) rounds?

answer.text: Each round at least halves the number of components

feedback.text: Correct — since every component merges with at least one other, the count at least halves.

answer.text: Each round removes exactly one edge from the graph

feedback.text: No — many edges are added per round, and components shrink geometrically.

answer.text: Each round doubles the number of components

feedback.text: Components decrease, not increase, each round.

answer.text: The number of rounds equals the number of edges

feedback.text: Rounds are logarithmic, far fewer than E.

generalfeedback.text: Because each component joins at least one neighbor, the number of components drops by at least half per round, giving O(log V) rounds.

questiontext.text: What is the overall time complexity of Borůvka's algorithm on a graph with V vertices and E edges?

answer.text: O(E log V)

feedback.text: Correct — O(log V) rounds, each scanning O(E) edges.

answer.text: O(V!) trying all spanning trees

feedback.text: Borůvka is polynomial and greedy, not brute force.

answer.text: O(V + E) with a single pass

feedback.text: There are O(log V) rounds, adding a log factor over one pass.

answer.text: O(E^2) from re-sorting edges every round

feedback.text: Borůvka needs no full sort; each round is a linear edge scan.

generalfeedback.text: Each of the O(log V) rounds scans O(E) edges to find every component's cheapest outgoing edge, giving O(E log V).

questiontext.text: Which practical feature most distinguishes Borůvka's algorithm from Prim's and Kruskal's?

answer.text: Its per-component, per-round structure makes it naturally parallelizable

feedback.text: Correct — all components can choose their cheapest edge independently and simultaneously.

answer.text: It is the only MST algorithm that ignores edge weights

feedback.text: No — Borůvka uses weights to pick each component's cheapest edge.

answer.text: It requires the graph to be directed and acyclic

feedback.text: No — MST algorithms work on undirected weighted graphs.

answer.text: It can only run on complete graphs

feedback.text: No — Borůvka works on any connected weighted graph.

generalfeedback.text: Because components make independent local choices each round, Borůvka maps cleanly onto parallel hardware — a key reason it remains relevant.

questiontext.text: Because each component selects its cheapest edge independently, Borůvka's algorithm is well suited to parallel implementation.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — independent per-component choices parallelize naturally.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Parallelizability is one of Borůvka's hallmark advantages.

questiontext.text: Borůvka's algorithm is historically the oldest of the well-known minimum spanning tree algorithms.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — Borůvka published it in 1926, before Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: It is indeed the oldest, predating both Kruskal and Prim.

questiontext.text: In each Borůvka round, the cheapest outgoing edge is chosen by every current ______ (single English word for a connected group of vertices; "component" or "supervertex").

answer.text: component

feedback.text: Correct — every connected component picks its cheapest outgoing edge.

answer.text: component*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: supervertex*

feedback.text: Correct — merged components are often called supervertices.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Borůvka's algorithm are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Each round at least halves the number of components, so it runs in O(E log V)

feedback.text: Yes — geometric shrinkage gives O(log V) rounds of O(E) work.

answer.text: It is naturally parallelizable because components choose edges independently

feedback.text: Yes — a defining advantage of Borůvka.

answer.text: It grows exactly one tree from a single start vertex using a min-heap

feedback.text: No — that is Prim; Borůvka merges many components at once.

answer.text: It processes one globally smallest edge per step and never merges in parallel

feedback.text: No — that resembles Kruskal; Borůvka adds many edges per round.

generalfeedback.text: Borůvka runs in O(E log V) by halving components each round and is naturally parallel; single-tree heap growth is Prim, and one-edge-at-a-time is Kruskal.
